references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where a disciple asks Jesus to first be allowed to bury his father before following him. Jesus answers: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead." This is the closest parallel to Luke 9:59.

The immediate context where another person says he will follow Jesus wherever he goes, and Jesus responds about the Son of Man's homelessness. This shows the pattern of calling and conditions for following Jesus.
Jesus' answer to the man in verse 59 and a third person who also wants to follow Jesus, but with reservations. Together these verses illustrate the radical nature of Jesus' call to discipleship.

Elijah calls Elisha to follow him. Elisha asks to be allowed to say goodbye to his parents first, which Elijah permits. Luke 9:59-62 can be seen as a deliberate parallel to this, where Jesus sets even stricter demands than the prophet Elijah.

Jesus teaches that whoever does not hate their father and mother and their own life cannot be his disciple. This underscores the radical demand to put Jesus before family obligations, the same theme as in 9:59.
Jesus says that no one can be his disciple without giving up everything. This expands on the theme that discipleship requires total devotion, without reservations – just like in the call in 9:59.
Jesus says that whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him. This sheds light on the same tension between family obligations and following Jesus as in Luke 9:59.
The calling of Levi, who left everything and followed Jesus. Levi's immediate response stands in contrast to the man's hesitation in 9:59, and shows what immediate obedience to Jesus' call entails.
